author: Jeffrey Eugenides
introFa: کتاب «Middlesex» نوشته Jeffrey Eugenides یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح C1 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «Middlesex»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

Wrenn), that has made a major contribution to Beowulf studies, especially since the full publication of the Sutton Hoo discoveries. The author is clearly and deeply infectiously interested in his theme, but of passion I can find no trace. This up-to-date and shrewd book must be regarded as a major contribution in its field, to which students at all levels will assuredly give a warm welcome. RUPERT BRUCE-MITFORD English Caroline Script and Monastic History: Studies in Benedictinism, A.D. 950-1030. By DAVID N. DUM- VILLE. (Studies in Anglo-Saxon History, 6.) 180 X 240mm. Pp.x+ 196, 5 tables, 16 pis. Wood- bridge, Suffolk, and Rochester, New York: The Boydell Press, 1993. £39.50. This book examines the history of English Caroline minuscule script and its connection with the Bene- dictine reform movement. Dumville builds upon many previous works, notably Neil Ker's Catalogue of Manuscripts containing Anglo-Saxon (1957) and T. A. M. Bishop's studies culminating in English Caroline Minuscule (1971). By its pioneering nature, Bishop's work on the script opened many ques- tions. Dumville addresses some of the issues, adds some up-to-date information and offers a his- torian's perspective, with many re-assessments of dating and localization, especially in favour of Bury St Edmunds and Canterbury. The book appears mainly to comprise two articles. The first concerns 'The Dissemination of Anglo-Caroline Minuscule' (chapter 11), with an Appendix. The second concerns the early history of the script at Canterbury (chapters III-IV). These are sandwiched by the Introduction and Conclu- sion (chapters i/v). More material is presented in footnotes than in the main text. To Bishop's original two styles of English Caro- line minuscule, Dumville adds a further two: Style HI, 'attributable to a brief period in the earlier eleventh century', confined to Worcester; and Style iv emerging at Christ Church c. 1020 and spreading rapidly. Dumville also recognizes 'various tran- sitional scripts' between styles (p. 108). His plea for increased recognition of 'this mixed history' (p. 147) is valuable. For definitions of Insular, Caroline and English Caroline minuscule the reader must turn to others' accounts or make infer- ences from Dumville's citation of features in indi- vidual scribes' works (as on pp. 24 and 129). Dumville's account of the styles sometimes seems inconsistent or confusing. The various accounts for the derivation of Style iv (pp. 5, 18, 28, 86 and 157) might not be equivalent. Nor need there be 'an exclusive fit between practice of one Anglo- Caroline style and membership of an identifiable group of houses' (p. 149), given the movement of scribes and circulation of exemplars. Although Dumville cites the textual content of manuscripts, he rarely remarks upon their format, layout or decoration, thereby divorcing script from related developments in decorated initials and the outline drawing style. The plates have varying quality and lack scales, making palaeographical comparisons difficult. The plate-captions refer back to the text, but not vice versa. Unsupported assertions that a book or hand is datable solely on palaeographical grounds (as on pp. 15, 30-1 and 38) do little to fulfill the perceived 'necessity to explain what is all too often left unstated or unorganised in palaeographical scholarship' (p. x). There is a recurring need to consult other works in tandem (such as Bishop's). Many statements require close checking against other pages in Dum- ville's text and the primary materials themselves. Within the book speculation becomes assertion becomes fact. For example, the reformation of Bury St Edmunds moves from: 'deductions . . . open up the possibility that' it was reformed by the 980s; through it 'seems to have been reformed' to it 'was reformed' by then (pp. 47-8 and 76-7, italics added). This frequent confusion of evidence and interpretation is indefensible. Such conditions make the book less helpful to 'new students' (p. ix) and tiresome for specialists. Dumville's challenging and thought-provoking suggestions could spur further refinements. Yet, with so many suppositions and hypotheses, the book cannot be regarded as definitive. Whether its assessments will endure, like many of Ker's and Bishop's, remains to be seen. Bishop's compacted prose is notoriously difficult to parse, and has misled some scholars in print. Dumville's diffuse, confusing and obfuscatory prose erects another barrier. As Dumville himself observes, 'crucial questions remain unanswered, manuscript mat- erial still awaits attribution, and a large mass of palaeographical data remains to be reexamined and analysed' (p. 110). MILDRED BUDNY and LESLIE FRENCH Aspects of Saxo-Norman London: I. Building and Street Development. By V. HORSMAN, C. MILNE and G.MILNE. 250mm. Pp.123, mills. London: London and Middlesex Archaeological Society, Special Paper n , 1988. ISBN0-903290-36-7. £'2-95

212 THE ANTIQUARIES JOURNAL Aspects of Saxo-Norman London: II. Finds and Environ- mental Evidence. Edited by A. VINCE. 250mm. Pp.451, 470 ills., 2 microfiches. London: London and Middlesex Archaeological Society, Special Paper 12, 1991. ISBN 0-903290-37-5. £39.95- Aspects of Saxo-Norman London: III. The Bridgehead and Billingsgate to 1200. By K. STEADMAN, T. DYSON and J.SCHOFIELD. 250mm. Pp.216, 74 ills., 1 micro- fiche. London: London and Middlesex Archaeo- logical Society, Special Paper 14, 1992. ISBNo- 903290-40-5. £27.00. Timber Building Techniques in London c.goo-1400. By G. MILNE. 250mm. Pp.152, 120 ills. London: London and Middlesex Archaeological Society, Special Paper 15, 1992. ISBN 0-903290-41-3. No price stated, pb. Post Medieval Pottery in London, 1500-1700, I. Border Wares. By J. PEARCE. 250mm. Pp. xii + 137, 66 figs. 11 col. pis. London: HMSO, 1992. ISBN0-11- 290494-7. £30.00. In presenting an extensive range of new data, these five reports bring considerable refinement to received wisdom and signal the application of many new approaches to the study of the City of London's past. They are important milestones in under- standing the City's development in the medieval and post-medieval periods. They demonstrate the very great significance of the work undertaken by the former Department of Urban Archaeology in the Museum of London, but they are also a testi- mony to the former imbalance in London between preservation or investigation on the one hand and destruction, even accompanied by watching briefs, on the other. Admittedly, circumstances had changed since 1975-6, when no archaeologists were permitted by the developers to monitor the Broken Wharf site. None the less, the obvious difficulties in recording evidence which lay outside the often minimal excavated areas reported here, the indica- tions of the amount which was consequently swept away virtually without record, and the over- stringent time constraints on many of the set-piece excavations, all emphasize the requirement for fur- ther change that existed until quite recently. Pearce's study of Border Wares uses both the Museum of London's collection as well as recently excavated material to present as comprehensive a type series as can possibly be constructed from the London occurrences of this Surrey/Hampshire ware. Even more obviously than with the other publications under review, it is really an interim statement, neither a complete history of the indus- try nor a full assessment of its significance. It proposes a sequence of development, evolving from the 'Surry Whitewares' already studied by Pearce and Vince in a LAMAS special paper, and chang- ing in response to new fashions in cooking and food preparation and the stimulus of imported ceramics. These influences are stated rather than introduced and discussed, and this reflects the apparent target readership, which must principally be fellow cer- amic experts and collectors. From the viewpoint of stimulating and informing the further research on this industry which is undoubtedly required, Pearce's analysis will undoubtedly form a constant point of reference. Each of the three fascicules of Aspects of Saxo- Norman London draws upon the relevant and avail- able data from an overall pool of sites. Seven exca- vations in the Billingsgate and Cheapside areas, where soil conditions militate against the preserva- tion of organic remains, provide the fifty or so structures which are described and analysed in Volume 1. Their dating is by reference to a chrono- logical framework of Ceramic Phases expounded in detail in Volume n; as research and publication progressed through the series, there was some refinement in the absolute dating of successive phases, which is summarized in Volume in. Many of the structures were very fragmentary, even in plan, but sufficient evidence was recovered to illus- trate four traditions of timber building which were used in the construction of two main types of buildings, 'surface-laid' and 'sunken-floored'. Ana- lysis of the form of structural detail, such as founda- tions, wall construction, floors, doors, partitions, etc., leaves some questions begging. For example, how were the roofs of some structures supported? The essays in reconstruction which follow further emphasize such problems, being positively pro- vocative in the assumptions which they require. Finally, the evidence for diversity in building tradi- tions, in form, and in position and density is used to develop theories about the nature and extent of pre-Norman settlement. The opening section of Volume 11 presents an analysis of the pottery evidence. It is in some ways fortuitous that most of the individual ceramic assemblages are small in size; Vince and Jones marshall this readily manageable corpus into a relative sequence of phases which underpins the archaeological interpretations elsewhere. This sequence alone is a measure of recent advances in our understanding. More than this, they use the pottery to hypothesize about the economic fortunes and influences of ninth to eleventh century London and to postulate some surprising metropolitan attributes. The difficulties which arise from the lack

REVIEWS 213 of precise dating, particularly for the century c. 850-950, are spelt out; economy of acknowledge- ment to source material, and occasional lapses in clarity of expression, make judgements on some other points more difficult to make. Unfortunately, the artefactual evidence presen- ted by Pritchard and her collaborators cannot con- tribute to the discussion of building form and function; this is a relatively small collection, much of it displaced and re-worked during later phases of site redevelopment. The paucity is well illustrated by the total of twenty iron knives which is described—compare the series of over two hundred from Coppergate, York, recently discussed by Ottaway. Nonetheless, this section is a valuable source of comparanda and information on an eclec- tic group of objects, which again is used to formu- late more general points about London's trade and contacts. The catalogue and discussion of 161 English and six foreign coins which follows includes all recorded single finds, whether from excavations, the Thames foreshore, or from soil dug out within the city but dumped elsewhere. Stott employs them to chart economic peaks, troughs, influences and contacts in an important essay which complements the work on pottery and artefacts. Equally, and perhaps more, remarkable is Archibald's commentary on Anglo-Saxon and Norman lead objects with official coin types, in which she postulates that the total of more than sixty items of this type from England, over half of which are from London, represent receipts for import duties. This innovative sug- gestion casts new light on the exercise of authority in the Anglo-Saxon period. Less exciting, because they are more routine and based upon relatively small data sets, are short sections on 'Plant Use and Biology' (largely a seed-based study), 'Parasite Remains', and 'Metal- lurgy' (principally analysis of crucibles). Vince rounds off the fascicule with an updated view of the 'Development of Saxon London'. Ignoring the irri- tations of omissions in the bibliography, in the figure referencing, and in the failure to cross- reference and correlate to other specialist contribu- tors such as Stott, this is a stimulating precis, both emphasizing gaps in current knowledge (the sixth to seventh centuries in particular) and proposing a variety of possible explanations for the changes in settlement patterns. Volume m presents the structural evidence from four sites on the waterfront, up- and down-stream of London Bridge. They are described against the background of a documentary overview which speculates incisively on the sequence of waterside development up to c. 1000. The ensuing site by site archaeological summaries, which occupy approxi- mately half of the volume, provide an appropriately detailed introduction to the patterns of successive reclamation and use; they are accompanied by high quality plans and photographs, although the use of more section drawings would have been useful in several places. In this fascicule, dendrochronology has been used to help refine the absolute dates of the Ceramic Phases proposed in the previous volumes; however, editorial control has not excised all inter- nal variations in the quoted ranges, as, for example, between pages 13 and 39. The remarkable sequences of embankments and timber structures which have been recorded permit a synthetic view of London's riverside develop- ment, which relates it to the evidence discussed in the two former volumes. There is informed specu- lation on the contemporary river regime, an essay which seeks to link riverside developments with the evolution of the local street system, and a conclud- ing summary discussion. Some weaknesses in the hierarchical format of the presentation, which have engendered a degree of repetition, and the lack of any overall plan showing all the main contemporary harbours, can- not diminish the enormous importance and value of this data. Its usefulness is enhaced through a series of Appendices incorporating a 'Finds Catalogue' in microfiche, a 'Tree Ring Analysis' which, although arguably an over-elaborate presentation of the data, includes important evidence for phases of building activity not recognized in situ, and an Index to the three volumes. Timber Building Techniques in London goo-1400 takes the structural evidence from the waterfront and employs it to expound the hypothesis that changes in waterfront construction are closely linked to and can illuminate changes in other timber building techniques for which direct evidence is rare or absent. Concentrating on the eleventh to thirteenth centuries, but with references to both earlier and later (seventeenth century) structures, the con- structional forms are well catalogued and excel- lently illustrated. The Milnes demonstrate how pragmatic consid- erations allow inferences to be made/ about tidal regimes, and reveal how, in each of the five site sequences which they studied, earthfast structures were superseded by framed structures in the early thirteenth century. They then suggest that framing evolved gradually from a fusion of attributes taken from otherwise separate traditions, with squared timber of uniform scantling and well-cut joinery seen in earthfast constructions by the twelfth

214 THE ANTIQUARIES JOURNAL century, and baseplates, a product of stave build- ing, known by the eleventh. The Billingsgate exca- vations in particular allow the study of re-used timbers; the recognition of a timber re-used for a second time some 200 years after its original use is a salutary warning to excavators. The volume con- cludes with an equally exciting breakthrough, Goodburn's use of the timbers to reconstruct contemporary woodland, its management, and the practice of carpentry, the latter accompanied by a particularly telling series of diagrams. Overall, these fascicules are well produced and well illustrated. In some places, as indicated above, they would have benefited from tighter editorial control; particularly in a series such as this, the use and definition of terms such as 'Saxo-Norman', 'early medieval' etc., should be standardized. It really would be better if'early medieval', confusing to British and Continental readers alike, was not used as a synonym for Saxo-Norman, or as a label for an extended Norman period. The four medieval volumes in particular are works with a significance far beyond the confines of London itself, both in their methodologies and in their results. No student of urban development, of the Anglo-Saxon era, of medieval timber building techniques, can afford to be ignorant of their data and conclusions. They have pin-pointed many areas which require further definition, discussion and elucidation. Amongst the more fundamental of these are the date range and reason for 'Black Earth' (cf. B. Yule, 1990, 'The 'dark earth' and late Roman London', Antiquity, 64, 620-8); the precise development of the settlement pattern within Cer- amic Phase 1, c. 850-1000, which itself needs to be dissected more finely; and the checking of the whole ceramic-based dating framework, which is overly reliant on relatively few data-sets. And there remain swathes of the late Saxon town, and par- ticular monuments such as the contemporary London Bridge, which urgently require further investigation. Above all, however, these fascicules succeed admirably in their stated aim of spreading information on vitally important new data, and thereby opening up new lines of analysis and interpretation. R. A. HALL From Viking to Crusader: Scandinavia and Europe 800-1200. Edited by ELSE ROESDAHL and DAVID M. WILSON. 270mm. Pp.429, 617 illus., maps, figs. Copenhagen: Nordic Council of Ministers in collaboration with the Council of Europe, 1992. ISBN 87-7303-5580^.). No price stated. This book is the catalogue prepared to accompany the international exhibition which, under various names, was held at Paris, Berlin and Copenhagen between April 1992 and March 1993. The cata- logue itself takes up 168 pages of the book and the remaining 60 per cent consists of a series of essays, indices, tables and maps which together provide an introduction to the archaeology and history of Scandinavia in the ninth to twelfth centuries and chart the relationship between Scandinavians and the rest of Europe during this period. Considering the large number of related exhibi- tions which have taken place in recent years and the wide scope of the exhibition (which included 617 catalogued items), the organizers and editors have had to steer a difficult course between producing an exhaustive catalogue to satisfy the specialist (and to make a contribution towards the academic study of the period) and producing a text which is accessible to the general reader and which summarizes existing knowledge. They have clearly veered towards the latter. Many of the exhibits will be familiar and the choice has clearly been made to show the best rather than the least well known artefacts of the period. As Olaf Olsen claims in his introduction, remarkably few of the requests for loan were refused, as one can see when leafing through the catalogue. The catalogue itself, however, is extremely com- pressed. Few entries are allowed more than a third of a page (as opposed to the two to three page entries allowed in The Work of Angels for the same artefacts) and many of the photographs are repro- duced at too small a scale to be of any real value. This deficiency is, however, more than outweighed by the introductory essays, arranged in three sections: 'Scandinavia and Europe', 'Culture and Society' and 'Artifacts and manuscripts'. These essays are uniformly excellent and are lavishly illustrated in colour. When one adds to them the extensive bibliography, which is organized both by subject and as a general bibliography, the location maps, and the outline chronology then one has here a very good way to approach the study of Scandinavia in the Viking Age. In summary, therefore, this catalogue manages to transcend the impermanent nature of its raison d'etre to pro- vide a survey of the archaeology of the Vikings at home and abroad which is wider-ranging geographically, in subject matter and its chrono- logical scope than any other source available in English. A. G. VINCE
